c.tagline: Coal city turned heritage capital — Buddhist grottoes, a hanging temple, and a reborn walled old town.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered (flagfall about ¥8); many drivers prefer cash or a Chinese mobile-pay QR code, and few speak English, so have your destination written in Chinese.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the police and 120 an ambulance; 119 is the fire brigade. English is rarely spoken, so ask your hotel to call on your behalf if possible.

hood_landmark.Datong Ancient City: Datong Ancient City Wall and Drum Tower

avoid.reason: Unofficial taxi touts cluster at the train station and Yungang Grottoes — agree fares in advance or use DiDi.

hood_desc: The heart of the visitor experience: a fully rebuilt Ming-era walled old town you can walk atop, packed with Huayan Temple, the Nine Dragon Wall, Shanhua Temple, the Drum Tower and lantern-lit streets. Best for first-timers who want the sights on their doorstep.

Datong's older commercial centre just outside the walls, built around Hongqi (Red Flag) Square with department stores, snack streets and Shanxi noodle joints; a lively, convenient base for shopping and eating.

The modern east-bank district of wide boulevards, government offices, and cultural landmarks like the new Datong Museum, Grand Theatre and library, plus international-brand hotels; calm, spacious and good for business travellers.

The southern edge of the city: the Kaiyuan Street area of newer residential blocks and chain hotels about 5 km below the old city, running southeast into the Shanxi Datong Economic Development Zone toward Datong South high-speed railway station and Yungang Airport. Quiet and practical rather than scenic, handy for an early train or flight.
lodging: Four Points by Sheraton Datong Pingcheng
Liuying Hotel (Datong South Railway Station Yungang International Airport Branch)

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as locals do; tap water is not potable.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:30 PM; after that Didi and taxis fill the gap. Sightseeing bus routes link the old city, railway station and the Yungang Grottoes.
transit.note: Datong has no metro or tram. Getting around is by an extensive city bus network, metered taxis, and the Didi ride-hailing app; the walled Ancient City itself is best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Bus fare is a flat ¥1-2, paid by scanning an Alipay or WeChat Pay QR code or with exact cash; there is no separate foreigner transit card, so link an international card to Alipay or WeChat for tap-to-ride.

bus: Intercity coaches to Taiyuan, Hunyuan (Hanging Temple) and Beijing

car.idp: Required (foreign licenses not valid; a temporary Chinese permit is needed)

food.desc: Ribbons of dough shaved straight off the block into boiling water with a curved blade, then dressed with braised pork, mutton or tomato and egg.

landmarks: Yungang Grottoes
Over 51,000 Buddhist statues, some 17 metres tall, fill 250 sandstone caves carved in the 5th century, a UNESCO masterpiece of early Chinese art.
Hanging Monastery (Xuankong Temple)
An impossible 1,500-year-old wooden temple clings to a sheer cliff on slender stilts 75 metres above the Jinlong canyon near Mount Heng.
Datong City Wall
The magnificently rebuilt Ming ramparts, 14 metres high and fully walkable, encircle the old town with gate towers spectacularly illuminated after dark.
Huayan Monastery
A rare Liao-dynasty temple complex whose vast Mahavira Hall and celebrated Bojiajiaozang library hall shelter exquisite 11th-century clay bodhisattvas.
Nine-Dragon Screen
China's oldest and largest glazed-tile dragon wall, 45 metres of writhing Ming-dynasty dragons built in 1392 for a prince's palace.
Shanhua Temple
A tranquil Tang-founded, Liao-Jin rebuilt monastery inside the south wall, prized for its sweeping timber halls and 24 celestial guardian statues.
Yingxian Wooden Pagoda (Sakyamuni Pagoda)
A day trip south stands the world's oldest and tallest wooden pagoda, 67 metres built in 1056 entirely without nails.
Mount Hengshan (Northern Heng)
One of China's five sacred Taoist mountains rises near the Hanging Monastery, its slopes stitched with temples, ridgeline trails and shrines.
Datong Drum Tower
A handsome three-storey Ming drum tower anchors the old town's main street, once beating the hours for the walled city.
Datong Museum
A striking swirl-shaped modern museum tracing the city's Northern Wei capital era, with dinosaur fossils, Liao treasures and Silk Road artefacts.

train.note: Datong has no international trains. High-speed services use Datong South, on the Datong-Zhangjiakou high-speed line towards Beijing and the Datong-Xi'an high-speed line running south past Taiyuan, putting Beijing within roughly two hours. The older Datong station in the city centre still handles conventional trains on the Beijing-Baotou and Datong-Puzhou lines, including overnight services towards Inner Mongolia. Book on 12306 with your passport, and check which of the two stations your train uses - they are a long way apart.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Datong. Long-distance buses run from the Xinnan (south) bus station to Beijing (about 4-5 hours), Taiyuan and Hohhot, and local and tour buses cover the Yungang Grottoes just west of the city and the Hanging Temple and wooden pagoda at Hunyuan and Yingxian. Tickets are bought at the terminal counter; for the grottoes the city bus is far cheaper than a tour.

ferry.note: Datong is a landlocked city on the dry loess plateau of northern Shanxi and has no passenger ferry services of any kind.

full.name: Mount Wutai
full.blurb: Sacred Buddhist mountain with clusters of ancient temples including Xiantong and Tayuan, one of China's four holy Buddhist peaks.

full.name: Yanmen Pass
full.blurb: Fortified Great Wall gateway that once guarded the frontier between central China and the Eurasian steppe.
